items.title: AMD and Meta Advance Strategic Partnership to Power Meta’s Superintelligence Infrastructure
items.content:
AMD and Meta Advance Strategic Partnership to Power Meta’s Superintelligence Infrastructure :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)
Press Release
AMD and Meta Advance Strategic Partnership to Power Meta’s Superintelligence Infrastructure
October 27, 2026 9:20 am EDT
Download as PDF
News Highlights
AMD and Meta collaborate across CPUs, GPUs, networking, systems and software to power Meta services and AI infrastructure
AMD Helios rackscale solutions will power Meta’s leading frontier models and services
AMD technology is the compute engine of choice for Muse and AMD technologies provide Day-0 support for leading Meta models
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Oct.  27, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today highlighted its deep strategic partnership with Meta, announcing AMD Helios™ rackscale solutions are running at Meta, AMD EPYC™ processors power Meta’s Muse AI agent, and AMD technologies provide Day-0 support for Meta models including Muse Spark Open and Muse Glimmer.
This builds on years of co-design and collaboration between the two companies across AMD EPYC™ processors, AMD Instinct™ GPUs, AMD Pensando™ networking and AMD ROCm™ AI infrastructure.
“Meta is a strategic partner for AMD, and we have built this partnership through years of deep technical collaboration – from EPYC processors powering Meta’s infrastructure to Instinct GPUs and open software supporting its AI workloads,” said Lisa Su, Chair and CEO, AMD. “With Helios now running at Meta, we are taking that partnership to a new scale in the superintelligence era. Together, we are building and deploying infrastructure at gigawatt scale and shaping future generations of silicon, software and systems to enable Meta’s most ambitious superintelligence models and services.”
“AMD has been a key partner in building out the compute that's running our frontier models,” said Mark Zuckerberg, founder and CEO, Meta, “We're making big investments in the computing power that will enable us to bring personal superintelligence to everyone, and AMD plays an important role in that.”
AMD Powering Meta Infrastructure, Today
AMD technology powers Meta’s infrastructure across compute, networking, systems and software.
Initial AMD Helios rackscale solutions are installed and being tested by Meta on the path to a broader deployment in the near future.
AMD EPYC processors support the dedicated computing environments behind Meta’s Muse personal AI agent. Meta has deployed millions of EPYC processors across multiple generations and is a lead customer for 6th Gen EPYC™ CPUs. The companies are also collaborating on future generations, including “Verano.”
AMD Instinct GPUs are currently used in production in Meta’s infrastructure for training, ranking and recommendation engines. Meta was also an early definition customer for the AMD Instinct™ MI450 architecture, and it will deploy a custom AMD Instinct GPU that is optimized for its workloads. The collaboration is also informing future AMD platforms, including AMD Instinct™ MI500 series GPUs and next-generation rack-scale systems.
AMD and Meta have worked together to advance ROCm through PyTorch to ensure that developers can leverage AMD GPUs right out of the box. As well, AMD delivered Day-0 support for Meta's Muse Spark Open models on AMD Instinct GPUs and for Muse Glimmer on AMD Ryzen™ AI PCs and AMD Radeon™ GPUs.
AMD and Meta have
expanded their software collaboration
to large-scale AI training, optimizing recommendation models on AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs and contributing improvements to PyTorch, Triton and ROCm for other developers to use.
As Meta grows its AI capabilities, the companies are working together across silicon, software and systems to address the demands of operating AI infrastructure for billions of people. The companies have aligned product roadmaps and engineering decisions around current and future Meta workloads, evolving years of collaboration into building and deploying integrated AI systems at gigawatt scale.
In addition, AMD will invest $1 billion in Meta’s equity offering.

items.content:
Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude \ Anthropic
Skip to main content
Chapter
01

Case studies
Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
Published
Oct 27, 2026
Team
Science
Anthropic’s
life sciences team
is working to accelerate curing disease. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines:
BigHat Biosciences
,
Bristol Myers Squibb
,
Divergence Labs
,
Enveda
,
Generate Biomedicines
, and
The Column Group
. We've also begun drug discovery efforts of our own. In doing so, we've learned a lot about how Claude can support drug development, and how we’ll need to improve Claude further to realize AI's potential in medicine. We plan to scale this work up substantially from here
.
There are many opportunities to speed up drug development, even beyond the most commonly discussed applications of AI, like
proposing initial designs
for new molecules. Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more.
Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks. There is no single problem to solve; the bottlenecks are distributed all throughout the drug development process. The best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs, across many different disease areas and stages of development.
So, over the past several months, we’ve partnered with six organizations to do so. We’ve also started drug discovery efforts of our own, including programs for rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, where Claude handles much of the scientific and operational work.
This work serves our goals in three ways. First, it lets us better understand the strengths and limitations of our models in relation to a much wider range of drug development tasks (we’ve already prioritized specific improvements to our models based on what we’ve learned so far). Second, these programs can serve as case studies for the wider life sciences community. If Claude is to significantly increase the rate of new cures, we need to work with many more biotechnology firms and integrate Claude more deeply into their development processes. Third, these projects should, if their positive trajectories continue, have direct impact themselves. We’re optimistic that some may result in effective new medicines for the diseases they target, including food allergies, rare childhood diseases, and several forms of cancer.
In this post, we provide an update on our progress with our partners, along with technical reports and preprints that describe our thought process, methods, and early results in more detail. We then briefly outline where our work is headed next.
Case studies
Generate Biomedicines: modality engineering.
Generate Biomedicines has been working on increasing the usefulness of a cancer treatment known as CAR T-cell therapy. This therapy has historically helped treat blood cell cancers; Generate aims to reengineer it so that it can treat solid tumor cancers too. To do this, they’re aiming to shorten one part of the therapy’s genetic instructions, which would create room for additional instructions suited to other kinds of cancer. Six Generate scientists used Claude Code to propose new designs for this part. One design was about 70% shorter than the standard version, and in lab tests it was more effective: it allowed immune cells to make roughly 10 times as many receptors (the proteins they use to spot cancer cells), it killed tumor cells more efficiently, and the immune cells remained active for longer.
Read more
, and see
Generate’s technical report
.
Divergence Labs: hit generation.
Divergence Labs is working on a novel way to treat food allergies. Food allergies are set off by a reaction from a molecule called IgE, some of which is attached to our immune cells and some of which floats freely in our blood. Divergence Labs is developing drugs that would detach the IgE from our immune cells entirely, rather than solely neutralizing the IgE circulating in our blood, as standard medications do. This could provide a much more effective treatment, but it requires a precise design, with two “arms”: one that would bind tightly to IgE, and another that would help prise IgE from the immune cell. Claude converted Divergence Labs’ goals into a detailed design plan, and then, largely autonomously, generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs in about a month to be narrowed down and tested. In those early tests, Divergence found “hits” for both arms: three designs that could bind to IgE, and 20 that could dislodge it. Three of those 20 appeared to dislodge IgE more than the standard medication. Its next step is to build a drug that combines the two arms.
Read more
, and see
Divergence’s technical report
.
BigHat Biosciences: lead optimization.
BigHat Biosciences pairs AI with an automated lab to improve potential drugs (or “leads”), which must bind their target tightly, remain stable through manufacturing and storage, and avoid clumping together (among other criteria). BigHat’s scientists and an Anthropic researcher worked with Claude to improve these three properties in two leads, both antibody fragments that could become parts of future drugs: one designed to target cancer cells, and one designed to keep a drug in the body longer. Claude, connected to BigHat’s lab data system, Reccy, proposed changes to each molecule, and BigHat’s lab made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks. Partway through, the team suspected the standard heat-stability and clumping metrics were misleading. Claude and the researcher reanalyzed the raw data, then proposed different metrics and a protocol change to test them. BigHat’s scientists refined and ran it, and the main predictions held. Compared with the originals, the best versions bound more than 10x more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution 18°C higher, and the lead for longer-lasting drugs clumped more than 100x more slowly.
Read more
, and see
BigHat’s technical report
.
Enveda: manufacturing and filings.
To conduct clinical trials, companies need records showing that each batch of a new drug has been made to strict quality standards, and to submit an application to regulators, among other requirements. At Enveda, manufacturing chemists spent up to 75% of their time on paperwork. To ease the load, Enveda built a system that connects all of its manufacturing documents to Claude, then lets Claude flag any possible issues. Over tests on 1,061 pages of documentation, Claude caught all 11 issues that human reviewers had spotted—and flagged seven they’d missed. In the process, this method reduced human review time by 89%, from over 25 hours to less than three. Separately, Claude wrote the first drafts of two important regulatory documents. One took four hours, compared to about three months by hand. For the other, Enveda’s standard human review process found one minor error.
Read more
, and see
Enveda’s technical report
.
The Column Group (TCG): company creation.
Because drug discovery can be slow, expensive, and prone to failure, investors in biotechnology companies have favored safer, previously validated ideas over riskier new ones, even when the latter could help more patients. We’ve been working with TCG to see whether Claude can change this by cutting the time and cost of drug discovery so that investors can confidently support more ambitious ideas. Specifically, TCG is establishing Pleiades, a new company that will use Claude to run many more—and more complex—drug programs than is usual for a small team. This could be a model for how Claude can reduce both the scientific and the operational and administrative overhead required to run a biotechnology company. If this works, this model could be replicated across the industry and direct investment toward harder problems in medicine. Pleiades is currently developing new tools and workflows for Claude; its very first Claude skill, which helps Claude assess whether drug targets are worth pursuing, has been evaluated on 45 target-disease pairs.
Read more
.
More recently, we’ve also begun working with
Bristol Myers Squibb
(BMS) to find and address bottlenecks in clinical trial planning. BMS is using Claude to assess plans of an early-stage drug in clinical trials, and to estimate the likelihood of those trials succeeding. Together, we plan to expand this work in 2027 to understand its potential for increasing the probability of success in early development.
“We use Claude at the clinical trial stage to analyze proprietary data, create a clinical study plan, and weigh the study’s chance of success. From a single prompt, Claude generated a robust initial analysis that helped inform our assessment of different development options, which would otherwise take days to complete. We did all of this while ensuring the security of our highly sensitive data. We look forward to expanding this work across our pipeline to support portfolio-level decisions.”
Michael Pourdehnad, MD
, Senior Vice President, Head of Early Clinical Development, Hematology, Oncology and Cell Therapy.
In addition to our work with these partners, we’ve begun to run some research programs ourselves. We’ve acquired Mithril Medicine, a one-person company that has been developing treatments for two rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Its founder, Cody Tranbarger, used Claude to organize contracts, logistics, and experiments with 11 external labs, and delegated many other aspects of Mithril’s operations to Claude. As a result, Mithril took a possible treatment for one form of muscular dystrophy from an idea to promising results in mice in less than 18 months. Now at Anthropic, Cody is continuing this research, and plans to start several new programs. If his drug candidates continue to hold up, we expect a drug to be ready to start clinical trials in humans as soon as late 2028.
Read more
and see
our technical report
.
Extending our work in the life sciences
All of this research is still at an early stage. In particular, so far it is mostly
preclinical—
that is, for the most part, it isn’t yet at the stage where the drugs are being tested in humans. We plan to continue extending Claude’s role into clinical trials as these drug programs advance, and as we partner with more organizations whose drug development programs are already at the clinical stage.
This research is only one part of our efforts to accelerate drug discovery. Ultimately, we want to share our models with as many drug development researchers as possible. To that end, we’ve rolled out
Claude Science
, our AI workbench for researchers, and we’re providing
Claude credits for life scientists
. We’ve also created the
Life Sciences Verification Program
to allow trusted organizations to use our most powerful models with more permissive versions of our safeguards, which are necessary to prevent misuse but which can impede legitimate biological research. We’ve also recently launched an
open call for guest investigators
in the life sciences; we’re seeking proposals from research groups who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in drug discovery and other areas.
We’re looking forward to working with many more organizations as we expand our life sciences research. If you work at an organization focused on drug discovery and are interested in collaborating with us, you can get in touch below.

Memory-Enforced GPU Sharing in Kubernetes with NVIDIA CUDA 13.4
Using the open-source GPU Fractioning Operator and KAI Scheduler to enforce per-workload memory limits at scale
Oct 27, 2026
By
Ekin Karabulut
,

and

AI-Generated Summary
GPU Fractioning Operator
is a new open-source Kubernetes operator hosted under the KAI Scheduler organization on GitHub.
It runs alongside the
NVIDIA GPU Operator
to set up and supervise Multi-Process Service (MPS) on every GPU node, apply per-workload memory limits and compute modes, and measure memory and compute use per GPU fraction rather than per whole GPU.
CUDA 13.4 introduces a memory boundary enforcement that is transparent to applications, offering exact memory amounts, guaranteed minimums with burstable maximums, and a choice between time-slicing and sm-sharing compute modes.
KAI Scheduler v0.18.0 integrates with GPU Fractioning through its NvFractions GPU-sharing mode, writing per-container Pod annotations that specify memory requests, limits, compute mode, and GPU device assignments for the operator to enforce on the node.
Administrators can enable NvFractions during KAI Scheduler installation with a Helm flag, and workloads declare fractional GPU requirements using annotations such as absolute memory sizes, portion-based fractions, optional burst limits, and compute mode selection.
Next Steps
Explore the
GPU Fractioning Operator repository
for installation and configuration instructions.
Review the
admin guide
and
user guide
for the three GPU sharing mechanisms.
Join the
Slack channel
or
bi-weekly community meetings
to ask questions and contribute.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
Many AI workloads need only a fraction of a GPU. Giving each one an entire device can leave capacity idle; sharing GPUs lets platform teams serve more workloads with the infrastructure they already have.
NVIDIA GPUs already support several approaches to sharing. Multi-instance GPU (MIG) splits a GPU into hardware-isolated instances that are transparent to the application, time-slicing lets several processes take turns without memory enforcement, and
Multi-Process Service
(MPS) lets them run concurrently in separate address spaces (sm-sharing).
CUDA 13.4 now enforces a memory boundary that is transparent to the application with a new time-sharing mode, alongside the compute sharing mode (sm-sharing) that already existed in MPS.
Here is what the
CUDA release
brings:
An exact memory amount:
A workload asks for a memory size and CUDA holds it there. An allocation above that size fails, just as it would on a smaller GPU.
A range:
A workload gets a guaranteed minimum plus a maximum it can grow into when memory is free.
A compute mode:
Each workload can choose to use its compute in an sm-sharing mode rather than using the default time-sharing mode.
A transparent memory limit:
Each workload sees only a fraction of the GPU memory.
The missing piece: Getting there from Kubernetes
CUDA provides the memory enforcement capability, but a Kubernetes cluster can’t use it on its own. On every GPU node, something has to:
Run and supervise the daemons that these features depend on
Apply each Pod container’s memory limits and compute mode before the process starts
Report what each fraction actually uses, rather than what the whole GPU uses
This work belongs on the node, independent of whichever scheduler placed the workload.
GPU fractioning: An open-source Kubernetes operator
A new open-source Kubernetes operator,
gpu-fractioning
, is  hosted under the
KAI Scheduler
organization on GitHub. It runs next to the
NVIDIA GPU Operator,
which provides the driver and the container runtime setup.
GPU Fractioning Operator handles three jobs:
It sets up and runs MPS on every GPU node.
It applies each workload’s memory limits and compute mode.
It measures memory and compute use per fraction rather than per GPU.
How schedulers pass GPU allocations to the operator
The developers write the resource and mode annotations in the pod YAML. Then the scheduler selects the GPUs for a workload and records its memory allocation and compute-sharing mode in per-container Pod annotations. GPU Fractioning Operator reads those annotations and configures the assigned GPUs to apply the workload’s memory limits and compute mode:
Annotation
Meaning
nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-memory.request
Guaranteed GPU memory
nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-memory.limit
Maximum the container may grow into
nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-compute.mode
time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing
nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpus.devices
Which GPUs the container was assigned
Table 1: Per-container Pod annotations that GPU Fractioning Operator reads to enforce a GPU fraction
Any Kubernetes scheduler that can write these annotations can enforce GPU fractions with CUDA. The scheduler still has its own job: choosing a GPU with enough free memory and never mixing compute modes on one GPU.
Using GPU Fractioning with KAI Scheduler
KAI Scheduler is the first scheduler integrated with
gpu-fractioning
. Starting with v0.18.0, KAI Scheduler has a GPU-sharing mode called
NvFractions
. KAI Scheduler picks which slice of which GPU each workload gets and writes the annotations (see Table 1, above), and
gpu-fractioning
enforces them on the node.
KAI Scheduler’s other sharing modes stay available, and administrators choose one per cluster. It can be enabled when KAI is installed:
helm upgrade -i kai-scheduler oci://ghcr.io/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler \
-n kai-scheduler --create-namespace \
--set global.nvFractions.set=true
This also installs
gpu-fractioning
as a dependency. From then on, you describe a fractional workload with Pod annotations.
There are four important annotations that answer four questions:
1. How much memory is needed
2. How far the workload may grow
3. How compute is shared
4. How many GPUs it spans
How much memory: The request
There are two ways to request memory:
1. As an absolute size:
Use the per-container NVIDIA annotation and standard Kubernetes units:
The container name (
app
) is part of the key, so it always targets the right container.
2. As a portion of a GPU by using KAI Scheduler’s existing annotation:
gpu-fraction: "0.5"
How far it may grow: The limit
This ability is new in KAI Scheduler. A workload can declare a guaranteed minimum (the request) and a maximum it may burst into when memory is free. Which limit annotation you use depends on how you wrote the request:
Request Type
Annotation
Example
Absolute Size
nvidia.com/container.<c>.gpu-memory.limit
“80Gi”
A Portion
kai.scheduler/container.<c>.gpu-memory.portion.limit
“0.8”
Table 2
:
Which limit annotation to use for each type of memory request
The limit is optional. If it is omitted, the limit equals the request and the workload is capped at exactly what it asked for. A portion limit must be greater than the
gpu-fraction
and less than 1.
How compute is shared: Time sharing or sm-sharing
Figure 1. Time-slicing divides the GPU’s time. SM-sharing divides its streaming multiprocessors (sm)
Compute can now be divided. Call n the number of workloads sharing a GPU: either way each gets roughly 1/n of the compute, and what differs is whether they take turns or run together.
Time-slicing is serial:
Workloads take turns on the whole GPU, and when every one of them uses its full slice each gets about 1/n of the time. Time left unused by one workload is shared equally between the others. This is the default. Each workload runs in its own error domain, i.e. full error isolation.
SM-sharing is parallel:
The GPU’s streaming multiprocessors (SMs) are split between workloads and all run at once, continuously. Nothing is carved out in advance. The GPU hardware allocates and releases SMs as workloads need them. When every workload is busy the split settles at roughly 1/n; when one goes quiet its SMs go to the others, and a single active workload can use them all. In this mode, workloads share a single error domain.
Compute mode is now explicit and can be set per container:
nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing"   # or "time-slicing"
A shared GPU runs one compute mode at a time, so KAI Scheduler never places a time-slicing workload and an sm-sharing workload on the same GPU. KAI Scheduler tracks this per GPU, not per node, so one node can host both modes on different GPUs.
How many GPUs are utilized
To get fractional capacity on several devices, add:
gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4"
The request applies to each device. A 40Gi request with four devices gets 40Gi on each of four GPUs.
Putting it together: Examples of GPU fractioning
An absolute size with room to burst on four GPUs with SM-sharing:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: inference
labels:
kai.scheduler/queue: default-queue
annotations:
nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.request: "40Gi"
nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.limit: "60Gi"       # optional
nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing" # optional, default time-slicing
gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4"                           # optional, default 1
spec:
schedulerName: kai-scheduler
containers:
- name: app
image: nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:13.0.2-base-ubuntu24.04
This is an inference server split across four GPUs that needs a guaranteed 40Gi on each GPU, can use up to 60Gi when neighbors are idle, and runs alongside other workloads instead of waiting its turn. SM-sharing puts the workloads in one error domain, so use it for workloads you trust to run together.
Half a GPU that may grow to 80% on two GPUs with time slicing (default):
metadata:
annotations:
gpu-fraction: "0.5"
gpu-fraction.limit: "0.8"  # optional
nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "time-slicing"    # optional
gpu-fraction-num-devices: "2"                                # optional
spec:
schedulerName: kai-scheduler
containers:
- name: app
This is an example for a development or batch job, such as notebooks or small fine-tuning runs, that need a guaranteed half of each of two GPUs and can grow to 80% when memory is free. Time-slicing gives each workload its own error domain, so a crash in one job doesn’t affect its neighbors. Running
nvidia-smi
in the container should show two GPUs, each with this workload’s fractional memory share.
Getting started
KAI Scheduler and the
GPU Fractioning
Operator are both on GitHub under
the KAI Scheduler organization
, with installation and configuration instructions for all three sharing mechanisms (See
admin
and
user
guides). Join
the Slack channel
or
bi-weekly community meetings
to ask your questions and contribute.
For more information about CUDA 13.4,
refer to the announcement.
You can also get involved during
KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026
in Salt Lake City, Utah

AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA RTX Spark
is a new Windows PC platform for AI development, creation, and gaming in slim laptops and compact desktops, combining up to 128 GB of unified memory with the full NVIDIA CUDA stack and RTX technologies including ray tracing and DLSS 5.
DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering runs on RTX Spark, starting with NBA 2K27, and an October model update runs 2x faster than the September version while halving GPU overhead and reducing VRAM use at 4K by 20%.
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB offers ~40% higher average quality against the prior model on relevant benchmarks and outputs up to ~80% fewer tokens versus peers, enabling responsive local AI character interactions on GeForce RTX and RTX Spark.
NVIDIA RTX Kit
brings eight neural rendering SDKs to RTX Spark, including RTX Neural Texture Compression, RTX Mega Geometry, and RTX Character Rendering for strand-based hair and skin with path tracing.
NVIDIA Nsight tools support graphics developer workflows across native Arm64, emulated x64, and Arm64EC applications on RTX Spark from day one, with Nsight Graphics 2026.3 introducing a Windows on Arm installer and Nsight Systems 2026.5 providing a single installer for all Windows versions.
The
NVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8
provides an updated foundation for advanced ray tracing and neural graphics in UE 5.8 projects, while MotionBricks adds new SOMA human-motion models, downloadable checkpoints, ONNX exports, and an interactive reference implementation built with Newton.
Next Steps
Download the
In-Game Inferencing (IGI) SDK
to access Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB for on-device AI characters.
Download
Nsight Graphics for RTX Spark
to capture, inspect, and profile frames for native Arm64 and emulated applications.
Explore the
RTX Neural Texture Compression repository
to integrate AI-powered texture compression into game projects.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
NVIDIA RTX Spark
is a new Windows PC platform for AI development, creation, and gaming in slim laptops and compact desktops. Powered by an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and NVIDIA Grace CPU, it combines up to 128 GB of unified memory with the full NVIDIA CUDA stack and RTX technologies including ray tracing and DLSS 5.
This post covers the following technologies for game developers building on RTX Spark:
DLSS
suite of technologies that boost FPS and improve image quality
NVIDIA ACE
updates for responsive, on-device AI characters
RTX Kit
SDKs for neural rendering, geometry, and character rendering
NVIDIA Nsight
tools for optimizing and debugging native Arm64 and x64 applications
NVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8
for integrating RTX technologies into your Unreal Engine projects
MotionBricks
update for human-character motion
DLSS on RTX Spark
RTX Spark benefits from the
full suite of DLSS technologies
in supported games, including Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, and 3D-Guided Neural Rendering.
DLSS Super Resolution reconstructs frames from a lower resolution input to improve performance. DLSS Ray Reconstruction generates additional pixels to enhance ray-traced scenes. DLSS Dynamic Multi Frame Generation can generate up to 5 additional frames per rendered frame, automatically adjusting the multiplier to maximize smoothness.
The latest
NVIDIA app beta
also brings a faster Performance Mode (Preset C) for Frame Generation, with minor trade-offs in image quality.
DLSS 5 brings 3D-Guided Neural Rendering to RTX Spark
DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering is supported on NVIDIA RTX Spark, starting with NBA 2K27.
An October model update runs 2x faster than the September version and halves GPU overhead while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. It also reduces VRAM use at 4K by 20%. The model will ship by default in future DLSS 5 games.
For developers, DLSS 5 adds a final stage to the graphics pipeline that enhances lighting and material detail. The engine-rendered frame, including artist-designed geometry, textures, and lighting buffers, remains the foundation, while developer controls determine what can change. Avalanche Software has taken advantage of DLSS 5’s SDK controls to tune the integration to maintain the artistic intent and style of the game.
Figure 1. Hogwarts Legacy with DLSS 5 off (left) and on (right)
Read the full DLSS 5 update
here
.
DLSS 4.5 Unreal Engine plugin
The updated
NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 plugin for Unreal Engine
gives developers powerful tools for delivering sharper images and smoother gameplay. Its second-generation transformer model for Super Resolution improves image stability, anti-aliasing, and visual clarity, while Ray Reconstruction enhances ray-traced image quality.
On supported GeForce RTX 50 Series and RTX PRO Blackwell GPUs, Dynamic Multi Frame Generation adapts the frame-generation multiplier as workloads change, with 6x Multi Frame Generation producing up to five additional frames per rendered frame.
A key addition in plugin version 8.9.0 is official Windows on Arm (WoA) support for Unreal Engine 5.8. Native ARM64 binaries and support for building and packaging UE 5.8 applications give developers a supported path to bring DLSS-enabled projects to RTX Spark systems. Alongside updated Streamline and NGX components and fixes for UE 5.8 Frame Generation issues, this release expands the plugin’s platform reach and helps developers prepare their applications for RTX Spark.
NVIDIA ACE introduces Nemotron 3.5 Bolt for on-device AI characters
NVIDIA ACE is our technology suite for creating in-game AI agents that deliver next-generation gaming experiences, and we’ve shared two exciting showcases this year:
PUBG rolled out AI teammates in a public beta powered by our first-generation Nemotron small language model (SLM). It helped new players land their first chicken dinners and generated viral clips across social media.
Aniimo debuted our more efficient second-generation Nemotron SLM, turning standard in-game pets into responsive AI companions that react to your voice. Players can check in on their pets’ feelings or teach them new tricks, which will bring a new level of immersion when it releases in early 2027.
More intelligence, less memory
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is now available. This model offers ~40% higher average quality against our prior model on relevant benchmarks and outputs up to ~80% fewer tokens vs peers.
It is purpose-built to power richer, faster in-game character interactions, with strong conversational capability,  autonomous multi-turn tool use, instruction adherence, and grounding to game state, all running locally on GeForce RTX and RTX Spark.
Figure 2. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt has best-in-class response quality and time to first token
Engineered for maximum intelligence and speed per GB of memory, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB enables responsive local experiences while preserving headroom for graphics rendering and local speech models. Key features include:
Multi-turn tool use
: Call application APIs to carry out tasks across a conversation, with integration guidance for asynchronous tool calls
Conversational mode
: Toggle to encourage concise, speech-ready responses for natural back-and-forth interactions.
Configurable reasoning
: Enable reasoning for complex requests or disable it for faster responses, with integration options to cap thinking to meet latency targets.
64k context
: Accommodate conversation history, instructions, tool definitions, retrieved information and game state.
Multilingual capability
: Support for 35 languages, building on a base model pre-trained on more than 140 languages.
Figure 3. Every NPC becomes an unscripted AI character. Here, the player asks Farkas: “Do you really trust the Jarl?”
Get started with NVIDIA ACE
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is available to developers via the
In-Game Inferencing (IGI) SDK
.
To test it in a game, check out SkyrimNET, an AI NPC modding platform by MinLL for
The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim
. SkyrimNET transforms every NPC into an unscripted, interactive character with personal memory, voice, and autonomy, enabling dynamic conversations and context-aware quests generated on the fly. The platform supports both cloud and local inference across multiple language models.
Download the SkyrimNET Plugin:
GitHub Repository
Download the ARM-Supported Loader:
Mod Organizer Release
NVIDIA RTX Kit brings neural rendering SDKs to RTX Spark
NVIDIA RTX Kit
brings neural rendering, complex geometry, and realistic character rendering to game development. Eight RTX Kit technologies are published with support for RTX Spark:
RTX Neural Texture Compression (NTC)
: Uses AI to shrink texture storage while maintaining visual fidelity comparable to traditional block compression.
RTX Texture Filtering
: Uses stochastic texture sampling after shading to reduce artifacts and improve image quality, including for difficult volumes.
RTX Neural Shaders
: Lets developers train neural networks and run them within shaders for new asset compression and approximation techniques.
RTX Mega Geometry
: Speeds up bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) construction for cluster-based geometry, helping developers ray trace more triangles and improve performance in complex scenes.
NVIDIA Real-Time Denoisers (NRD)
: Provides denoisers for diffuse and specular lighting and shadows, producing cleaner images from low ray-per-pixel inputs.
RTX Character Rendering
: Provides tools for rendering strand-based hair and skin with path tracing, including subsurface scattering and Blackwell-accelerated hair primitives.
RTX Global Illumination (RTXGI)
: Provides several techniques for efficient indirect lighting for ray traced and path traced applications.
Opacity Micro-Maps (OMM)
: Used to accelerate ray tracing of high detail geometry by efficiently encoding the opacity states of micro-triangles and micro meshes.
Optimizing and debugging RTX Spark applications
NVIDIA Nsight tools are ready for RTX Spark from day one, supporting graphics developer workflows across native Arm64, emulated x64, and Arm64EC applications.
Nsight Graphics lets developers capture, inspect, and profile individual frames, examining every draw call, shader, and resource to diagnose rendering bugs and tune GPU performance. Nsight Graphics release 2026.3 introduces a new Windows on Arm installer for RTX Spark systems, supporting native Arm64 target applications as well as emulated x64 and Arm64EC targets.
Nsight Systems delivers a system-wide view of application performance, correlating CPU threads, GPU workloads, API calls, and memory activity on a single timeline so developers can pinpoint bottlenecks and balance work across the platform. Starting with Nsight Systems 2026.5, a single installer for all versions of Windows supports both native Arm64 and emulated applications.
Nsight Aftermath helps teams resolve GPU crashes and hangs by generating detailed crash dumps that show what the GPU was doing at the moment of failure, both during development and in the field. Nsight Aftermath SDK 2026.3 includes a Windows on Arm version for integrating into native Arm64 applications. Crash dumps from emulated x64 applications will continue to function as expected with the x64 version of the SDK.
Download Nsight Graphics for RTX Spark
here
Download Nsight Systems for RTX Spark
here
Download Nsight Aftermath SDK for RTX Spark
here
NVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8
The release of
NVIDIA RTX Branch of Unreal Engine 5.8 (NvRTX 5.8)
gives developers an updated foundation for bringing advanced ray tracing and neural graphics to UE 5.8 projects. This update focuses on codebase refactoring, stabilization, and compatibility improvements. Developers can access the branch source through GitHub to integrate and customize NVIDIA RTX technologies for their games and applications.
Simplify runtime character animation with MotionBricks
Figure 4. MotionBricks generates pose-guided character motion in an Unreal Engine research demonstration
MotionBricks is open-source research for generating character motion in real time. Rather than hand-authoring every transition and wiring it into an increasingly complex animation graph, developers guide motion through target poses. MotionBricks generates the connecting movement at runtime and adapts as player input or game event changes.
Paper
GitHub
The model supports control over speed, direction, and movement style, along with pose-guided interactions such as sitting and picking up objects. These capabilities let developers build varied character behaviors through a common pose-based interface. The original research demonstration shows these behaviors working together in Unreal Engine.
Research demonstrations
The update builds on this work with:
New SOMA human-motion models
, alongside the existing G1 robot model.
Downloadable checkpoints, ONNX exports, and export tools
for developers building their own integrations.
An interactive reference implementation built with Newton
, demonstrating pose-guided human and robot motion.
MotionBricks is provided as research code and models. The Unreal Engine integration shown in the research demonstration is not included in this release.

items.title: Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats A2UI now supports swappable inference formats, introducing A2UI Express which uses up to 3x fewer tokens and cuts latency by c
items.content:
Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats
- Google Developers Blog
Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats
OCT. 27, 2026
Vishal Motwani
Vibes Builder
Google A2UI Team
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
We've heard your concerns about the speed of A2UI and generative UI experiences: people wait while the model generates each screen. This release gives you levers to make that faster, so you can choose the trade-off that fits each screen.
With this release, we’re happy to introduce swappable inference formats and share examples on leveraging decision models with A2UI, which help building faster and more reliable generative UI experiences. Using our new A2UI Express as an inference format you can reduce latency by up to
3x
, and up-to
80x
using decision models like Jev to make layout decisions. Express requires up to 3x fewer tokens to generate the same kinds of UI compared to Direct JSON. We'll dive into the details in this blog post.
A2UI is an agent-optimized protocol for generative UI, where a client advertises a catalog of trusted components as a contract, an agent sends A2UI messages describing a bespoke user interface composed from that catalog, and the client's renderer draws the UI (see
Introducing A2UI
).
Initially agents generated A2UI JSON transport messages directly, every curly brace and nested element. It turns out that generating JSON trees constrained by a complex JSON schema is slow and error-prone for LLMs. This coupled A2UI to LLMs, which output text, and made it difficult to integrate faster System One decision models.
Now agents can generate
A2UI Express
, an intermediate format optimized for inference speed and accuracy, and rely on deterministic code in A2UI's Agent SDKs to translate it into the JSON-based transport protocol. Agent builders are also free to swap in any other DSL and its associated compiler for any special use-cases, and our A2UI Agent SDK(s) make it compatible with transports and renders.
The format the model generates is what we call
inference_format
. You set it with one argument when you create the generator. The SDK generates the prompt instructions for that format and compiles the model's reply into standard A2UI messages. This post covers how the swap works, why we developed A2UI Express as the new default inference format, and how a decision model can build screens from layouts you define in advance.
Two things no longer true about A2UI
How swappable inference formats work
An inference format has two parts, and the SDK generates both from your catalog's JSON schema. A prompt section teaches the model the format's syntax, and a compiler compiles the model's reply into validated A2UI messages. Because both come from the schema, a format can't describe a component or property that your catalog lacks.
You choose the format with one argument when you create the generator:
from a2ui.processor import A2uiGenerator, CatalogConfig
from a2ui.inference_formats import ExpressFormatFactory
catalog = CatalogConfig.from_path("catalog.json")
generator = A2uiGenerator(
[catalog],
examples=few_shot_examples,  # written once as A2UI JSON
inference_format_factory=ExpressFormatFactory(),
)
processor = generator.create_processor(renderer_capabilities)
system_prompt = f"{instructions}\n\n{processor.prompt_snippet}"
parts = processor.parse_response(model_reply)  # text parts + validated A2UI messages
Python
Copied
A2UI Express is available in the Python agent SDK (
a2ui-agent-sdk
0.9.0 on PyPI), in the TypeScript agent SDK (
@a2ui/agent
on npm), and in the Dart SDK (
a2ui_agent
0.0.1-wip004 on pub.dev). In TypeScript, you pass
new ExpressFormatFactory()
as the generator's third argument. The Python and TypeScript SDKs can both stream Direct JSON chunk by chunk, and they compile Express from the complete reply.
Express: the same screens in a third of the tokens
Express writes one statement per line, in a style close to Python. Each line assigns a component to a variable, and the variable name becomes the component ID. Arguments are positional: the compiler maps them to property names in the order your catalog schema declares them, and _ skips one. $/title binds a value to the data model, and
Event("accept")
declares a server action. This is the A2UI gallery's notification card in Express:
surface("gallery-notification-permission")
$/description="Get alerts for order status changes"
$/icon="check"
$/title="Enable notification"
root=Card(main_column)
main_column=Column([icon, title, description, actions], _, "center")
icon=Icon($/icon)
title=Text($/title)
description=Text($/description, "body")
actions=Row([yes_btn, no_btn], "center")
yes_btn_text=Text("Yes")
yes_btn=Button(yes_btn_text, _, Event("accept", {}))
no_btn_text=Text("No")
no_btn=Button(no_btn_text, _, Event("decline", {}))
Plain text
Copied
Swappable Inference formats including A2UI Express also work with macros in the Python agent SDK, which help when a screen shows data your systems already hold. The model writes a call with only an ID, such as
OrderStatus("ord_42")
, and your macro fetches the order and fills in the values, so every value on screen comes straight from your data. The
macros README
shows the setup.
How we devised A2UI Express
Customer feedback uncovered latency and accuracy issues with direct JSON generation. To fix this, we started devising a new inference format. We experimented with four options:
Direct JSON
: This was our existing baseline that we launched with back in December 2025.
Express
: The final `python` syntax inspired format that we picked as the new default.
Atom
: Writes Lisp-style S-expressions with no assignments and no closing tags.
Elemental
: Writes HTML with custom elements, betting on how well models already write HTML.
We ran all four formats through the same 51-task eval on gemini-3.5-flash and compared them for thinking modes: on and off.
We observed that Express inference format works just as well even with thinking off; which can give you the fastest inference times when working with A2UI Express.
Controlled generation with Jev
Some screens have a known shape, such as a settings page, a checkout or a confirmation. For those, the model doesn't need to design a layout. It needs to choose among layouts you have already defined, and a different kind of model is built for that. For this, you would not need the full expressivity provided by A2UI Express.
Jev
, from TypeSafe, is what is called a
System One model
, built to make fast, structured decisions that code can use directly. Jev doesn't generate text or JSON. You send it a state and a set of typed questions, and it answers each one with calibrated probabilities. A question can ask whether a statement is true (Noul), which option from a list fits (Choice), or how something scores on a rubric (Score). Jev answers many questions in one request, in roughly 100 to 300 ms.
Apparite
(jev2ui), an open-source design tool, shows one way to connect a System One model to A2UI. Jev decides the structure of each screen, code builds the A2UI components from those decisions, and a small model, gemini-3.5-flash-lite, writes only the text. The questions live in a Markdown grammar written ahead of time. A blockquote asks a question, and the bullets are its options, each with criteria. This block from
grammar/screen.md
decides which control a settings row gets:
#### row_control (of each row in rows, within each group in groups)
Material: a switch for one on/off setting that takes effect at once. HIG: a disclosure indicator for a row that opens another page.
> `{row}` is a row in the supplied screen and section. Grouped rows can represent content, navigation, settings or actions; use their actual text and context to decide.
>
> What kind of row is {row}?
- **switch** — A setting that is simply on or off and takes effect at once: notifications, dark mode, autoplay, sync.
- **value** — A setting with one current value picked from several, changed on another page: language, quality, theme, frequency, units.
- **nav** — A link to another page: a content item, details, account, privacy, help, about, or managing something. Its text and section identify what it opens.
- **check** — One of several alternative options listed together, of which one is chosen: the choices of a single setting, such as '10 seconds', '30 seconds', 'High', 'Low'.
- **danger** — A final or destructive account action: sign out, delete account, clear data, reset.
Plain text
Copied
On a podcast app's settings screen, Jev answers
Skip forward
→ value,
Auto-download
→ switch and
Log out
→ danger, each at p ≈ 1.00. Apparite builds a whole screen in three steps:
One Jev request answers the grammar's layout questions, about 30 for a screen.
Code builds the component tree from the catalog and sends
createSurface
and
updateComponents
at about 200 ms, with placeholders where the text will go.
gemini-3.5-flash-lite streams the text into
updateDataModel
. As each part arrives, small follow-up Jev requests settle what depends on it, such as the row controls above.
In one run of 11 prompts, the component tree was on screen in 92 to 298 ms and each screen was complete in 0.8 to 1.7 s. The text writer generated 101 to 341 tokens per screen, and both of Apparite's Jev pipelines produced valid A2UI on all 11 prompts. The project treats these numbers as a first look, since the sample is small.
Controlled generation can only produce the layouts its grammar describes. Apparite's grammar covers nine screen archetypes and twelve blocks, so screens without a known shape are a better fit for Express. A2UI Agent SDKs, don’t include a decision model inference format yet;
apparite(jev2ui)
project is an example on how A2UI messages could be assembled given a batch of independent decisions from a decision model.
Which mode to use
A2UI Express is fast and keeps the full expressivity of A2UI, but a decision model making multiple independent decisions is still faster. Choose by how much of the screen you can define ahead of time:
Controlled, when a decision model can produce what you need.
If your screens follow set and defined layouts, a decision model may be the fastest option.
Express for full expressivity.
When a screen needs more expressivity based on your catalog, fall back to A2UI Express. It's fast, and the model still writes the whole component tree.
Your own format for anything new.
Because inference formats are swappable, a new use case or a future syntax needs only a prompt generator that teaches the model your DSL and a converter that converts between your DSL and A2UI messages. Your catalog and renderers stay the same.
Try it
Use Express in your agent.
Install the Python SDK with
pip install a2ui-agent-sdk
or the TypeScript SDK with
npm install @a2ui/agent
, pass
ExpressFormatFactory()
when you create the generator, and run the model with thinking off. Your catalog and renderers stay as they are, and the
Express specification
documents the syntax.
To teach Gemini, or any other model that loads skills, to write Express with only your components, generate skills from your catalog with the Python SDK's
SkillGenerator
:
import json
from a2ui.core import Catalog
from a2ui.inference_formats.express import ExpressFormat
from a2ui.skill import SkillGenerator
catalog = Catalog.from_json(json.load(open("catalog.json")))
skills = SkillGenerator(ExpressFormat([catalog])).generate_skillset()
skills.export_to_directory("skills")  # a2ui-core plus one skill per catalog
Python
Copied
Try controlled generation.
Clone the
example jev2ui repository
, and follow the instructions there to get started. A hosted version of
Apparite(jev2ui)
runs at
apparite.cnfg.ai
.
Sources
Earlier A2UI posts:
Introducing A2UI
(December 2025),
A2UI v0.9
(April 2026) and
A2UI + MCP Apps
(June 2026).

and
A2UI Atom specification

in the A2UI eval

Introduction: From Blueprint to Working Prototype
Imagine ordering your weekly groceries as naturally as texting a friend:
"Hey, we're out of milk and eggs. Can you also add some snacks for Friday movie night?"
In our previous post,
Building Conversational Commerce with Multi-Agent Swarms on GCP
, we shared the architectural blueprint for conversational commerce—proposing a 3-layer decoupled design (Ingress, Memory, and Cognition) to solve messaging timeouts, state tracking, and response reliability.
While blueprints establish the architecture on paper, production readiness demands working software. In this post, we take that blueprint and bring it to life with a functional prototype called
HappyDelivery
.
Using
LangGraph
,
Gemini
,
FastAPI
, and
Google Cloud
, we'll walk through the code, the state machine, deterministic financial tools, and an automated verification suite that demonstrates how this multi-agent swarm operates in practice.
1. The Prototype Stack: 3 Layers, 3 Diagrams
To build a reliable commerce swarm, we implemented three decoupled layers that handle the journey of every customer text message:
Let's examine how each layer functions in code with its own dedicated architecture.
Layer 1: Ingress Layer (Omni-Channel Webhook Gateway on GKE/Cloud Run + Cloud Pub/Sub)
A frequent question when designing conversational commerce is:
how does a message sent by a customer on their smartphone actually land in Layer 1, and can this architecture support messaging platforms beyond WhatsApp?
How Client Devices Connect to Layer 1
End users do not communicate directly with your Google Cloud servers. Instead, customer messages traverse an operator ecosystem before landing on your webhook:
Supporting Multiple Messaging Channels: WhatsApp, RCS, Apple Messages, and SMS
Every major consumer messaging platform operates on the exact same fundamental contract:
an asynchronous HTTPS POST webhook delivery with a strict HTTP acknowledgement timeout
:
WhatsApp (Meta Cloud API)
:
Requires a prompt
HTTP 200 OK acknowledgement
and validating the
X-Hub-Signature-256
header against your Meta App Secret using HMAC-SHA256. If your server times out or returns a non-200 status, Meta marks delivery as failed and initiates exponential backoff retries (for up to 7 days), which can trigger duplicate order deliveries.
Google RCS Business Messaging (RBM)
:
Delivered via Google Cloud Pub/Sub push or HTTPS webhooks authenticated via OAuth2 / Service Account JWT bearer tokens or payload HMAC signature verification (
X-Goog-Signature
). Requires returning
HTTP 200
promptly to avoid webhook delivery retries.
Apple Messages for Business (AMB)
:
Delivered through an Apple-approved Messaging Service Provider (MSP). Authenticated via provider webhook signatures, JSON Web Signatures (JWS), or Mutual TLS (mTLS) with prompt
HTTP 200 OK
acknowledgement expectations.
SMS / MMS (
Twilio
,
Sinch
,
Infobip
):
Standard form-encoded or JSON POST webhooks signed with vendor-specific HMAC tokens (e.g.,
X-Twilio-Signature
).
While the payload schemas and cryptographic headers differ slightly between platforms,
Layer 1 abstracts away all client differences
:
Security & Signature Verifier:
Routes incoming requests through platform-specific signature validators (
MetaHmacValidator
,
RcsJwtValidator
,
AppleJwsValidator
,
TwilioHmacValidator
).
Payload Normalization Adapter:
Ingests vendor-specific payloads and transforms them into a unified, channel-agnostic canonical schema (
CommonMessageEvent
):
{
"channel": "whatsapp",  # or "rcs", "apple_messages", "sms"
"sender_id": "+1xxxxxxxxxx",  # Verified E.164 phone number
"text": "Out of milk & eggs",
"timestamp": 1773428900,
"raw_metadata": {...}
}
Python
Copied
Sub-150ms Asynchronous Handshake:
Queues the canonical message onto Google Cloud Pub/Sub and returns
HTTP 200 OK
in
< 150ms.
This ensures the rest of your system—Session Store (Layer 2) and Agent Swarm (Layer 3)—operates on clean, normalized data without caring whether the shopper sent their message from an iPhone, an Android RCS chat, or a WhatsApp thread.
Layer 2: Session & Cart Layer (Cloud Memorystore Redis)
Messaging platforms are completely stateless: every text message arrives as an isolated webhook event. To provide a coherent shopping experience, the system must instantly reconstruct the customer's full context without having to re-read or re-parse days of chat logs on every turn.
We use
Cloud Memorystore (Redis)
keyed by the customer's verified phone number (session:{phone_number}) to store active state:
Real-World Customer Journeys (CUJs) Powered by this Layer
The Asynchronous Shopping Trip (Pause & Resume):
In real life, people don't complete an order in one sitting. A customer might text at 9:00 AM:
"Add a gallon of milk to my cart"
, close WhatsApp to catch a train, and reply at 2:00 PM:
"Also add bread and eggs, and what's my total?"
Because session state is cached in Redis, the system instantly restores their active cart ([Milk]) and recalculates totals without losing a beat.
Contextual Guardrails (Dietary Preferences & Addresses):
If a user's profile specifies
dietary_preferences: ["Nut-Free"]
, the Inventory Agent automatically respects that preference when recommending movie night snacks—without the user having to re-declare their allergy in every text message.
Safe, Tokenized Checkout:
The customer profile holds tokenized payment references (
customer_id: "cust_9821", payment_ref: "Visa ending in 4242"
). The LLM only ever reads the friendly masked label, while the transaction tools pass the tokenized customer ID to Stripe. Raw credit card numbers never touch chat prompts or logs.
💡 Scale & Performance: What QPS Can the Base Infrastructure Handle?
A common question in conversational commerce is whether state lookups will introduce latency. Here is what the baseline infrastructure supports:
Raw Throughput:
A single, baseline
Google Cloud Memorystore for Redis
instance (Basic Tier, 1–5 GB memory) easily delivers
10,000 to 50,000+ QPS
with sub-millisecond (< 1ms) read/write latencies.
Conversational QPS:
Each chat turn requires 2–3 Redis operations (session fetch, cart mutation, state commit). This means a single standard Redis instance comfortably handles
3,000 to 15,000 active conversational turns per second
before needing Redis Cluster horizontal sharding or read replicas.
Memory Capacity:
An active session payload (profile + active cart + preferences) takes ~2 KB to 5 KB of serialized JSON. A modest 5 GB Redis instance can hold
over 1,000,000 concurrent active shopping carts
in memory simultaneously.
Key Takeaway:
In practice, the Session & Cart Layer will
never be the bottleneck
—it easily outpaces upstream webhook inference and downstream LLM inference.
Layer 3: Agent Swarm Layer (Multi-Agent Orchestration with Gemini)
Rather than relying on a single monolithic prompt to handle every task, we separate reasoning into a swarm of specialized agents:
Supervisor (Gemini Flash):
Acts as a low-latency router, classifying the customer's request and delegating it to the right specialist.
Profile Specialist:
Retrieves personal preferences and issues secure single-use auth links for new buyers.
Inventory Specialist (Gemini Pro):
Bound to warehouse tools; queries stock, recommends pairing items, and mutates the cart.
Transaction Specialist (Gemini Pro):
Bound to payment tools; calculates totals deterministically and initiates charges.
2. From Architecture to Code: Building the 3 Layers
Now that we have seen the high-level design of the three layers, let's look at the actual Python prototype code that brings each layer to life.
Layer 1 Prototype: Omni-Channel FastAPI Ingress & Security Normalization
The goal of this service is simple:
verify authenticity across any inbound channel, normalize the payload into a canonical schema, and get off the critical path in < 150ms
.
Here is our implementation showing how multiple messaging channels (WhatsApp, RCS, Apple Messages, SMS) are handled by pluggable adapters:
import hashlib, hmac, json, time
from typing import Any, Dict, Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel
class CommonMessageEvent(BaseModel):
"""Channel-agnostic canonical representation of an inbound customer message."""
channel: str  # "whatsapp", "rcs", "apple_messages", "sms"
sender_id: str  # E.164 phone number: "+1xxxxxxxxxx"
text: str
timestamp: float
raw_metadata: Dict[str, Any]
class HappyDeliveryIngressService:
"""Omni-Channel FastAPI Ingress with cryptographic verification and async queueing."""
def __init__(self, meta_secret: str, rcs_secret: str = ""):
self.meta_secret = meta_secret
self.rcs_secret = rcs_secret
self.publisher = CloudPubSubPublisher()
def verify_whatsapp_signature(self, payload_bytes: bytes, sig_header: str) -> bool:
"""Verifies X-Hub-Signature-256 header using constant-time comparison."""
if not sig_header or not sig_header.startswith("sha256="):
return False
expected_hash = hmac.new(
self.meta_secret.encode("utf-8"), payload_bytes, hashlib.sha256
).hexdigest()
provided_hash = sig_header.split("sha256=")[1]
return hmac.compare_digest(expected_hash, provided_hash)
def normalize_payload(self, channel: str, raw_payload: Dict[str, Any]) -> Optional[CommonMessageEvent]:
"""Extracts sender and message text into a canonical schema."""
if channel == "whatsapp":
# Meta Graph Webhook structure
entry = raw_payload.get("entry", [{}])[0]
change = entry.get("changes", [{}])[0].get("value", {})
message = change.get("messages", [{}])[0]
return CommonMessageEvent(
channel="whatsapp",
sender_id=message.get("from", ""),
text=message.get("text", {}).get("body", ""),
timestamp=float(message.get("timestamp", time.time())),
raw_metadata={"message_id": message.get("id")},
)
elif channel == "rcs":
# Google RCS Business Messaging structure
return CommonMessageEvent(
channel="rcs",
sender_id=raw_payload.get("senderPhoneNumber", ""),
text=raw_payload.get("text", ""),
timestamp=time.time(),
raw_metadata={"rcs_message_id": raw_payload.get("messageId")},
)
return None
def handle_incoming_webhook(
self, channel: str, payload: Dict[str, Any], signature: str
) -> Dict[str, Any]:
"""Validates signature, normalizes schema, and offloads to Pub/Sub in < 150ms."""
payload_bytes = json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")
# 1. Platform-specific security validation
if channel == "whatsapp" and not self.verify_whatsapp_signature(payload_bytes, signature):
return {"status": "error", "message": "Invalid HMAC signature", "http_code": 403}
# 2. Normalize to canonical schema
event = self.normalize_payload(channel, payload)
if not event or not event.sender_id:
return {"status": "error", "message": "Unrecognized payload format", "http_code": 400}

Preview, edit, and collaborate on markdown (.md) files natively in Google Docs and Drive
- Google Developers Blog
Preview, edit, and collaborate on markdown (.md) files natively in Google Docs and Drive
OCT. 26, 2026
Sophia Siao
Product Manager
Chelsea Rice
Senior Product Manager
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Google Workspace is bridging the gap between code and collaboration by providing a familiar, real-time environment where developers and AI agents can seamlessly work together on documentation.
Markdown (.md) is a standard text format widely used by LLMs to preserve structured content—such as tables, headers, and bulleted lists—without the overhead of bulky file formats. Markdown file usage in Google Drive has surged year-over-year, indicating how critical this format has become for modern, fast-paced workflows.
Now, you can natively view, edit, and collaborate in markdown files directly in Google Docs, eliminating the friction of manual file conversions. You can edit without changing file types while ensuring your underlying documentation is preserved for developer tools and git repositories. Plus, with rendered previews in Google Drive, you can easily review formatting with a click.
Built for human and agent collaboration
As AI agents take on larger roles in drafting, planning, and coding, markdown serves as a collaborative common language between humans and AI tools because it is easily readable by both. Google Docs provides a familiar, easy-to-use environment, acting as a shared bridge where team members and autonomous agents work together directly on the same documents. When you open a markdown file in Google Docs, you have:
Native file fidelity:
Manage and edit .md files directly in Google Docs without converting them into a different format. A visible .md badge in the document header clearly indicates you are working in a native markdown file.
Real-time collaboration:
Teammates and AI agents can co-edit the same file to maintain a single source of truth across engineering, product, and AI tools. You can also leverage Google Docs commenting to leave real-time, line-level feedback and track suggestions.
Tracked version history:
Maintain a complete, transparent audit trail of all revisions made across both human contributors and AI agents.
Storage in Drive:
Preview rich, formatted markdown files directly inside Drive—with full support for tables and hyperlinks—or seamlessly toggle to raw text without needing a separate viewer.
Link to Youtube Video
(visible only when JS is disabled)
By combining the simplicity of markdown with the powerful real-time collaboration of Google Docs, teams now have a unified workspace to draft, review, and ship technical content faster.
Availability
Anyone with a Google or Workspace account can get started today by uploading an .md file to Google Drive and begin collaborating directly in Google Docs.

Uber rival inDrive eyes 2027 robotaxi tests in Central Asia with Pony AI and Nvidia
Jagmeet Singh
9:00 PM PDT · October 22, 2026
Ride-hailing company
inDrive
, known for letting passengers and drivers negotiate fares, is working with Chinese autonomous driving firm Pony.ai and Nvidia to begin testing robotaxis in Kazakhstan in 2027.
The companies said Friday that they had signed a memorandum of understanding to explore bringing Pony.ai’s robotaxis to inDrive’s platform — a reflection of the growing interest in self-driving technology beyond the U.S. and China.
Testing will begin in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana, in the first half of 2027, inDrive CTO Yuri Misnik told TechCrunch. The tests will initially involve a safety operator, with fully driverless rides as the eventual goal.
Under the proposed plan, Pony.ai would provide its Gen-7 robotaxis, which inDrive would offer through its ride-hailing app and operate in Kazakhstan. Nvidia, on the other hand, would supply the AI technology, including its Hyperion platform and Halos safety system.
The move comes as ride-hailing companies expand their push into robotaxis. Earlier this month, Uber announced plans to
test Pony.ai’s robotaxis in London
, where it has also started offering supervised autonomous rides with British startup Wayve, an
investor-backed partner
. Uber is also working with multiple robotaxi companies in other markets, including the Middle East.
Having built its business around affordable rides, inDrive is now looking to bring a similar focus to autonomous ride-hailing as it explores a market where Uber and other rivals are already making moves.
“Our approach is capital-light by design,” said Misnik. “We work with a range of partners in different markets, combining their expertise with ours to deliver a better customer experience.”
Nvidia says its Hyperion platform could lower the cost of developing robotaxis by giving companies a ready-made foundation of sensors and computing technology, rather than requiring them to build and integrate everything themselves. The company also offers its Alpamayo model and tools to generate synthetic data and test autonomous driving systems across different driving scenarios.
“Those savings are particularly relevant in emerging markets, where ride-hailing is already relatively affordable and autonomous services need to compete on cost,” Ali Kani, Nvidia’s vice president of automotive, told TechCrunch.
The announcement coincides with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s first visit to Kazakhstan on Friday.
The Kazakhstan proposal would also add to Pony.ai’s ongoing push beyond China. The company aims to have
more than 3,500 robotaxis
operating in over 20 cities worldwide by the end of 2026, up from a fleet of 1,975 vehicles at the end of June.
Last month, Kazakhstan
announced
plans to launch autonomous taxi services in 2027, with initial trials planned in Astana and two other cities. It has also introduced rules for autonomous vehicles to be tested on certain public roads.
Astana’s harsh winters could make it a useful testing ground for robotaxis. The city, with a population of around 1.7 million, faces months of snow and ice, posing challenges for autonomous driving systems.
“Launching here will provide an important opportunity to evaluate autonomous driving technology in challenging winter conditions,” inDrive founder and CEO Arsen Tomsky said. “Success in Astana could offer valuable insights for expanding autonomous mobility to other locations facing similar challenges.”
Kazakhstan is not the only market where inDrive is exploring robotaxis. In December, the company signed a separate agreement
with Saudi Arabia’s AI Driver
to explore deploying autonomous vehicles powered by Chinese self-driving firm WeRide, starting with Riyadh. The companies had targeted a pilot in the first half of 2026, though it remains unclear whether testing has begun.
“We are also looking at a number of other markets for future deployments,” said Misnik. “One of the main requisites for successful launch in our view is a favorable and collaborative regulatory environment to facilitate safe and sustainable testing on the roads.”
The company operates in more than 1,200 cities across 47 countries and has
expanded beyond ride-hailing
into delivery, intercity transportation, and financial services.
